title: What you believe
hookLine: Judaism has room for many beliefs; write yours honestly
tomorrow: belief is half of it. which of the things you do are yours?

cards: College roommate forms ask the oddest things. Night owl or early bird. Neat or messy.
And at the bottom of Noa's: anything about your beliefs we should know? One blank box. Where would anyone start?
Jewish tradition has an old answer, and it begins with a gesture: a hand over the eyes.

teach.h: HEAR, O ISRAEL: THE LORD IS ONE.
teach.b: The line is the Shema: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one."
The Talmud tells that Rabbi Judah the Prince passed his hand over his eyes when he said it, and people still cover their eyes for that line. It's the center: shut out the noise, say the one thing.
But around that center, Judaism has argued about belief for a long time. Maimonides set out principles of faith in his commentary on the Mishnah.
Later thinkers, Joseph Albo among them, pushed back and drew up a different list.
When two great schools of sages disagreed, the Talmud said of them both: these and these are the words of the living God. So the tradition gives a center and a wide, argued-over room around it.

Writing your beliefs honestly fits that room. Some will be firm, some brand new, some still being tested. Something to tell a friend tonight: covering your eyes for the Shema goes back to one line about one rabbi's hand.

how: It is a Jewish custom to cover the eyes with a hand while saying the first line of the Shema, morning and night; Jewish thinkers from Maimonides on have written, and argued about, statements of belief.

o: the things you hold true, written honestly
the opinions your family handed to you
the list every member must sign to join

p: hear, O Israel: the LORD is one

s: Judaism has no beliefs, only practices

covering the eyes for the Shema goes back to a story in the Talmud

games.q: your nephew asks at dinner: 'is believing every line in the prayer book required to be Jewish?' what fits today?
o: there's a center, the Shema, and Jews have argued about the rest for ages.
yes; there's one fixed list, and doubting any line puts you outside.
no; belief doesn't come into it at all, only food and family do.
games.why: Maimonides wrote principles, others argued with his list, and the Talmud says 'these and these.' an honest kid's question fits right in.

practice: Cover your eyes with one hand, the way people do for the Shema, and stay there for a few slow breaths.
Then, on paper and by hand, write three sentences that start with "I believe": one you're sure of, one you're growing into, one you're still testing.

wordCard.voice: What you believe: the things you hold true, written honestly, around the Shema's center and in the tradition's wide room.

orig.note: Hebrew: hear, O Israel, the first words of Deuteronomy 6:4.

carryVoice: For the road: your beliefs, half-sure ones included. That's day one of your own path.
